# Nonnegative regression

In alternating optimization, 

$$
\min_{W \geq 0, H\geq 0} \|Y - WH^T\|_F^2
$$

fixing all but one factor turns a nonnegative LRA problem into a nonnegative regression problem.

$$
\min_{W \geq 0} \|Y - WH^T\|_F^2
$$

:::{style ="text-align:center; font-size=130%;"}
**Today: understand this optimization problem and the algorithms that solve it.**
:::

## From a matrix to a vector problem

The problem is separable rowwise,

$$
\| Y - WH^T \|_F^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \| Y[i,:] - W[i,:]H^T\|_2^2.
$$

We need to minimize a quadratic form for each rows $W[i,:]:=x$, leading to solving $m$ problems of the form

$$
\min_{x\geq 0} \| y - Ux \|_2^2.
$$



## Nonnegative regression

Given observations $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and a dictionary $U \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$:

$$
\min_{x \geq 0} f(y, Ux).
$$


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}



- $x$: nonnegative coefficients
- $Ux$: reconstructed observation
- $f$: separable, convex loss in its second argument

Two losses will organize the lecture:

- Euclidean distance: **NNLS**
- Kullback-Leibler divergence: **NNKL**
:::

::: {.column}

![](../figures/nnlsU.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

:::

:::




## Why nonnegativity matters

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Interpretation

Without constraints, least squares gives

$$
x_{\mathrm{LS}} = U^\dagger y.
$$

Negative coefficients can be difficult to interpret as abundances, intensities...

- Question: is this clear to everyone ?

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Solution uniqueness and properties

Nonnegativity is an informative prior:

- underdetermined problems can still have unique solutions
- solutions are naturally sparse
- feasible reconstructions form a cone

:::
::::

# NNLS: the Euclidean case

## Problem formulation

The nonnegative least-squares problem is

$$
\boxed{\text{NNLS:}\quad x^* \in \arg\min_{x \geq 0} \|y - Ux\|_2^2 \quad}
$$

- It is a convex quadratic program.
- A solution always exists (projection on a convex set, see next slide)
- There is generally no closed-form formula.

For full columns rank matrix $U$, the projected estimate $[U^\dagger y]^+$ is generally **not** the NNLS solution.

## NNLS as projection on a cone

Define the cone generated by the columns of $U$:


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}


$$
\mathcal{C}(U) = \{Ux : x \geq 0\}.
$$

Then NNLS can be written as

$$
\min_{z \in \mathcal{C}(U)} \|y-z\|_2^2.
$$

The reconstructed vector $z^*=Ux^*$ is the orthogonal projection of $y$ onto the cone.

:::

::: {.column}



![](../figures/Nnlsproj2.png){fig-align="center" width="72%"}


:::

:::

When $y$ lies outside the cone, its projection often lands on a lower-dimensional facet. The corresponding coefficient vector $x^*$ is sparse.


:::{style="text-align:center; font-size:130%;"}
::: {.callout-caution}

The actual shape of the cone depends on matrix $U$. Most of the intuition in this masterclass assumes that $U$ is nonnegative.

:::
:::

## KKT conditions

The geometry gives intuition. The KKT conditions transform this intuition into a set of equations.

Consider the Lagragian

$$
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda) = \|y-Ux\|_2^2 - \langle \lambda,x\rangle,
$$

an optimal pair $(x^*,\lambda^*)$ satisfies

$$
\begin{aligned}
&x^* \geq 0, \qquad \lambda^* \geq 0,\\
&\lambda^*[i]x^*[i] = 0,\\
&2U^T(Ux^*-y)-\lambda^*=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

These conditions separate active coefficients from inactive ones.

## KKT conditions on the support

Let $S = \operatorname{supp}(x^*)$ and $r^* = y-Ux^*$.

On the support:

$$
U[:,S]^T r^* = 0.
$$

Outside the support:

$$
U[:,S^c]^T r^* \leq 0.
$$

So the active atoms are orthogonal to the residual.


:::{style="text-align:center; font-size:130%;"}
:::{.callout-tip}

If the optimal support is known and $U[:,S]$ is invertible, the solution can be computed exactly!

$$ U^T[:,S]U[:,S]x^\ast = U^T[:,S]y $$

:::
:::

## The night-sky theorem


:::{style="text-align:center; font-size:130%;"}
::: {.callout-tip}
### Theorem

If $y \notin \mathcal{C}(U)$ and $\operatorname{spark}(U)>m$, then NNLS has a unique solution with

$$
|\operatorname{supp}(x^*)| \leq m-1.
$$

:::
:::

This is the **night-sky theorem**:

- an underdetermined NNLS problem can have a unique solution.
- the solution is sparse even without an explicit sparsity penalty.
- knowing the support reduces the problem to least squares.


#### Proof elements

- The residual cannot be null, and is uniquely defined.
- The condition $U[:,S]^T r^* = 0$ imposes that columns of $U[:,S]$ are in the orthogonal space of $r^\ast$, of dimension $m-1$.
  - Thus $U[:,S]$ is also always full column rank, and there exists a solution with a support of size at most $m-1$.
- If there are no groups of $m$ colinear colums (the spark condition), then $S$ is unique, and so is $x^\ast$.

## NNLS recap


NNLS is simultaneously:

- a constrained quadratic program.
- a projection onto a convex cone.
- a support-estimation problem.


Its algorithms will exploit one of these three viewpoints. We will explore them in a second part of the talk.

# NNKL: the Poisson case

## Why replace the Euclidean loss?

The Euclidean loss treats absolute errors equally across the signal range.


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

For data with large dynamic range or count measurements:

- small values may be scientifically important
- variance can grow with the signal
- relative error can matter more than absolute error

A Poisson model gives a different data fidelity term.


:::

::: {.column}

$$ (100 - 101)^2 = 1$$

$$ (1-2)^2 = 1 $$

:::

:::




## NNKL problem formulation

For Poisson observations (distribution of counting things),

$$
Y[i] \mid x \sim \mathcal{P}((Ux)[i]),
$$

maximum likelihood leads to the generalized KL divergence

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(y,z)
= \sum_i y[i]\log\frac{y[i]}{z[i]} + z[i]-y[i].
$$

The nonnegative KL regression problem is

$$
\boxed{\text{NNKL:} \quad x^* \in \arg\min_{x \geq 0} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(y,Ux). \quad}
$$

## KL divergence in one dimension

The scalar KL divergence is minimized at $q=p$.

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p,q)=p\log\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)+q-p.
$$


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}




For the reference value $p=2.5$, the curve is:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

q = np.linspace(1e-5, 10, 300)
p = 2.5
kl = p * np.log(p / q) + q - p

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
ax.plot(q, kl, color="#1f77b4", linewidth=2.5)
ax.scatter([p], [0], color="#d00000", zorder=3)
ax.axvline(p, color="#d00000", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.set_title("Scalar KL divergence")
ax.set_xlabel("q")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$D_{KL}(p,q)$")
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```


:::

::: {.column}

$$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(100,101) = 100\log(100/101) + 1 \approx 0.005 $$

$$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(1,2) = \log(1/2) + 1 \approx 0.31  $$
$$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(2,1) = 2\log(2) - 1 \approx 0.39  $$


:::

:::

## NNLS and NNKL: different geometries

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

**NNLS**

$$
\|y-Ux\|_2^2
$$

- quadratic
- orthogonal projection
- closed form solution if the support is known

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

**NNKL**

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(y,Ux)
$$

- Poisson likelihood
- non-Euclidean projection
- no closed-form even with support (see later)

:::
::::

## Difficulty 1: curvature near zero

The KL curvature is

$$
\frac{\partial^2 D_{\mathrm{KL}}(y,z)}{\partial z^2}
= \frac{y}{z^2}.
$$

It becomes unbounded as $z \to 0$.

Consequences:

- No global Lipschitz constant for the gradient: $\forall y\geq 0, \;\forall L \geq 0,\; \exists z \geq 0 \text{ s.t. } \|\nabla_x D_{\mathrm{KL}}(y,z)\| > L\|z\|$.
- No universally safe fixed gradient step.
- Sparse data can make first-order methods inefficient.

## Difficulty 2: no strong convexity

KL divergence is strictly convex, but generally not strongly convex: for large $z$, it becomes asymptotically linear.


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

<br>
<br>


- gradient methods need not have a global linear rate
- large dynamic ranges make the problem harder
- zeros in $y$ create broad linear regions


:::

::: {.column}



![](../figures/Lipschitz.png){fig-align="center" width="90%"}


:::

:::

## Difficulty 3: the support is not enough

On a known support $S$, the NNKL KKT equation is

$$
U[:,S]^T\left(1-\frac{y}{Ux^*}\right)=0.
$$

:::{style ="text-align:center"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.optimize import minimize

U = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 3.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
y = np.array([6.0, 1.0, 2.0])


def kl_obj(x):
    z = U @ x
    return np.sum(y * np.log(y / z) + z - y)


res = minimize(kl_obj, x0=np.array([1.0, 1.0]), bounds=[(1e-6, None)] * 2)
x_star = res.x
z_star = U @ x_star
residual_star = 1 - y / z_star

x1 = np.linspace(1e-2, 3, 300)
x2 = np.linspace(1e-2, 3, 300)
X1, X2 = np.meshgrid(x1, x2)
Z1 = U[0, 0] * X1 + U[0, 1] * X2
Z2 = U[1, 0] * X1 + U[1, 1] * X2
Z3 = U[2, 0] * X1 + U[2, 1] * X2
KL = (
    (y[0] * np.log(y[0] / Z1) + Z1 - y[0])
    + (y[1] * np.log(y[1] / Z2) + Z2 - y[1])
    + (y[2] * np.log(y[2] / Z3) + Z3 - y[2])
)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))

levels = np.linspace(KL.min(), np.percentile(KL, 60), 20)
cs = ax1.contour(X1, X2, KL, levels=levels, cmap="viridis")
ax1.clabel(cs, inline=True, fontsize=7)
ax1.scatter(*x_star, color="#d00000", zorder=3, label=r"$x^*$ (facet $x_2=0$)")
ax1.set_title(r"Parameter domain: $D_{KL}(y,Ux)$")
ax1.set_xlabel(r"$x_1$")
ax1.set_ylabel(r"$x_2$")
ax1.legend(loc="upper right")
ax1.grid(alpha=0.2)

# view of the same objective through the first two output coordinates (y1,y2)
M = U[:2, :]
Minv = np.linalg.inv(M)
z1 = np.linspace(1e-2, 8, 300)
z2 = np.linspace(1e-2, 8, 300)
Y1, Y2 = np.meshgrid(z1, z2)
Xz1 = Minv[0, 0] * Y1 + Minv[0, 1] * Y2
Xz2 = Minv[1, 0] * Y1 + Minv[1, 1] * Y2
Y3 = U[2, 0] * Xz1 + U[2, 1] * Xz2
with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
    KL_z = (
        (y[0] * np.log(y[0] / Y1) + Y1 - y[0])
        + (y[1] * np.log(y[1] / Y2) + Y2 - y[1])
        + (y[2] * np.log(y[2] / Y3) + Y3 - y[2])
    )
KL_z = np.where(Y3 > 0, KL_z, np.nan)

t = np.linspace(0, 3, 50)
ray1 = np.outer(t, U[:2, 0])
ray2 = np.outer(t, U[:2, 1])

levels_z = np.linspace(np.nanmin(KL_z), np.nanpercentile(KL_z, 60), 20)
cs2 = ax2.contour(Y1, Y2, KL_z, levels=levels_z, cmap="viridis")
ax2.clabel(cs2, inline=True, fontsize=7)
ax2.fill(
    np.r_[0, ray1[:, 0], ray2[::-1, 0]],
    np.r_[0, ray1[:, 1], ray2[::-1, 1]],
    color="#1f77b4",
    alpha=0.1,
    label=r"model cone $\{Ux : x\geq 0\}$",
)
ax2.plot(ray1[:, 0], ray1[:, 1], color="#1f77b4", linewidth=1)
ax2.plot(ray2[:, 0], ray2[:, 1], color="#1f77b4", linewidth=1)
ax2.plot(
    [y[0], z_star[0]],
    [y[1], z_star[1]],
    color="#555555",
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=1.2,
    zorder=2,
)
ax2.scatter(y[0], y[1], color="#2ca02c", zorder=3, label=r"$y$ (outside cone)")
ax2.scatter(
    z_star[0],
    z_star[1],
    color="#d00000",
    zorder=3,
    label=r"$Ux^*$ (on facet)",
)
ax2.set_title(r"Image domain: $D_{KL}(y,z)$")
ax2.set_xlabel(r"$y_1$")
ax2.set_ylabel(r"$y_2$")
ax2.set_xlim(0, 8)
ax2.set_ylim(0, 8)
ax2.legend(loc="upper right")
ax2.grid(alpha=0.2)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"y = {y}, Ux* = {z_star}, residual 1-y/(Ux*) = {residual_star}")
```
:::

Here $y$ lies outside the model cone $\{Ux : x\geq 0\}$: solving the KKT equation on the full support $\{1,2\}$ would give a solution violating nonnegativity, so the true projection $Ux^*$ falls on a facet of the cone ($x_2=0$), leaving column 2 inactive. Even locating the solution on this facet requires solving an optimization problem.

## Bonus trick: optimal scaling for NNKL

Consider scaling a candidate reconstruction by $\alpha$:

$$
\min_{\alpha \geq 0} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(y,\alpha Ux).
$$

At the optimum,

$$
\alpha^* = \frac{\sum_i y[i]}{\sum_i (Ux)[i]}.
$$

Thus any optimal solution satisfies

$$
\sum_i (Ux^*)[i] = \sum_i y[i].
$$

When columns of $U$ sum to one, the model and data have matching marginals.

# Three algorithmic viewpoints

## Which algorithm for which problem?

| Method | NNLS | NNKL | Main idea |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--|
| Active-Set | yes | no | search for the support |
| HALS | yes | no | exact coordinate blocks |
| Multiplicative Updates | yes | yes | scaled first-order steps |

The best method depends on the shape of the regression:

- one vector or a matrix of right-hand sides?
- Euclidean or KL loss?
- sparse solution or dense iterates?

# Active-Set for NNLS

## Active-Set: search for the support

If the support $S$ were known, NNLS would reduce to

$$
\min_{x[S]} \|y-U[:,S]x[S]\|_2^2.
$$

Active-Set (AS) alternates between:

1. adding a promising atom
2. solving least squares on the active support
3. removing coefficients that violate nonnegativity


## Step 1: select an atom

With residual $r=y-Ux$, choose the inactive atom most correlated with $r$:

$$
j = \arg\max_{i\notin S} \langle U[:,i],r\rangle,
\qquad S \leftarrow S \cup \{j\}.
$$

- This follows the KKT condition: at optimality, correlations vanish on the support and are negative outside it.
- Other perspective: choose the column of $U$ that is most correlated with the residual, likely to "explain" the remaining data the best.

## Step 2: solve on the active support

Compute the unconstrained restricted least-squares solution

$$
z[S] = U[:,S]^\dagger y,
\qquad z[S^c]=0.
$$

- If $z \geq 0$, accept it and continue with the next iteration. Stop if KKT conditions show optimality.
- If some entries of $z$ are negative, the candidate is infeasible, go to step 3.

## Step 3: return to the feasible cone

Move from the current feasible point $x$ toward $z$:

$$
 x \leftarrow x+t(z-x),
$$

with the largest feasible step

$$
 t^* = \min_{i:z[i]<0}\frac{x[i]}{x[i]-z[i]}.
$$

- At least (an often exactly) one coefficient reaches zero, so the support is reduced.
- The cost decreases along the segment $(x,z)$ by convexity!
  - This guarantees that the same support is never visited twice, since all operators in AS reduce the cost, and a given support leads to a fixed residual error.

Then go back to step 2.

## Summary of Active-Set

![](../figures/active_set.png){fig-align="center" width="50%"}

## Active-Set: what is guaranteed?

Every accepted step decreases the NNLS cost.

A support is not revisited unless the optimum has been reached. Therefore AS terminates after finitely many support changes, although the worst-case number of supports is exponential.

AS is especially attractive when:

- the unknown is a single vector
- the solution is sparse
- initialization is close to the solution

# HALS for matrix NNLS

## Why Active-Set does not scale to batches

Matrix NNLS is

$$
\min_{H^T\geq 0} \|Y-WH^T\|_F^2.
$$

Each column of $H^T$ is a separate NNLS problem, potentially with a different support.

Solving restricted linear systems independently is expensive.

:::{style="text-align:center; font-size:130%;"}
:::{.callout-tip}

## HALS strategy

Work on rank-one terms, alternatively.
:::
:::

## HALS: the matrix view

![](../figures/hals.png){fig-align="center" width="72%"}

HALS is exact alternating optimization:

- each row update decreases the objective
- all right-hand sides are updated together
- with nonzero columns of $U$, convergence is to the global NNLS minimizer

Lecture 3: we will implement HALS to compute NMF and Nonnegative Tucker decomposition!

## The one-dimensional NNLS building block



::: {.columns}

::: {.column}


For $a \neq 0$ and $Z$ fixed,
$$
\arg\min_{h\geq 0}\|Z-ah^T\|_F^2
= \left[\frac{a^TZ}{\|a\|_2^2}\right]_+.
$$

Each entry is just a scalar quadratic minimization:

$$
 h[i] = \max\left(0,\frac{a^TZ[:,i]}{\|a\|_2^2}\right).
$$
:::

::: {.column}


![](../figures/nnls1d.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

:::

:::




## HALS update

To update row $j$ of $H^T$, remove its current contribution:

$$
Z = Y - U[:, -j]H^T[-j,:].
$$

Then update the whole row at once:

$$
H^T[j,:]
\leftarrow
\left[\frac{U[:,j]^TZ}{\|U[:,j]\|_2^2}\right]_+.
$$

This is an exact minimization over one block, because the cost is separable with respect to entries in a single row.


# Multiplicative Updates

## A common update pattern

Multiplicative Updates (MU) preserve nonnegativity by construction:

$$
 x^{(k+1)} = x^{(k)} \ast \frac{\text{nonnegative numerator}}{\text{nonnegative denominator}}.
$$

For NNLS:

$$
 x^{(k+1)} = x^{(k)}\ast
 \frac{U^Ty}{U^TUx^{(k)}}.
$$

For NNKL:

$$
 x^{(k+1)} = x^{(k)}\ast
 \frac{U^T\left(y/Ux^{(k)}\right)}{U^T1}.
$$

All products and divisions are elementwise.

## MU as a gradient ratio

The gradients can be split into positive and negative parts:

$$
\nabla f = \nabla^+ f - \nabla^- f.
$$

Then MU has the mnemonic form

$$
 x^{(k+1)} = x^{(k)}\ast
 \frac{\nabla^- f(x^{(k)})}{\nabla^+ f(x^{(k)})}.
$$

At a stationary point, the ratio tends to one wherever $x>0$.

## MM: optimize a majorant

At the current iterate $x^{(k)}$, build a surrogate $\xi(x,x^{(k)})$ such that

$$
\xi(x,x^{(k)}) \geq f(y,Ux),
\qquad
\xi(x^{(k)},x^{(k)}) = f(y,Ux^{(k)}).
$$

Then take the next iterate by minimizing the surrogate:

$$
x^{(k+1)} \in \arg\min_{x\geq 0} \xi(x,x^{(k)}).
$$

The important design goals are **global upper-bounding**, **tightness**, and a tractable minimization.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

![](../figures/Mmprinciple.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

The majorant touches the cost at $x^{(k)}$ and is easier to minimize. Its minimizer gives a guaranteed descent step.

:::
::::

## Jensen constructs the majorant

Jensen's inequality gives

$$
f\left(y[i],\sum_j\lambda_{i,j}u_{i,j}\right)
\leq \sum_j\lambda_{i,j}f(y[i],u_{i,j}).
$$

Convexity turns one coupled loss into a sum of simpler losses.

Let

$$
\hat y[i] = (Ux^{(k)})[i],
\qquad
\lambda_{i,j} = \frac{U[i,j]x^{(k)}[j]}{\hat y[i]}.
\qquad
u_{i,j}=\frac{x[j]}{x^{(k)}[j]}\hat y[i].
$$

For each observation $i$,

$$
\sum_j \lambda_{i,j}=1,
$$

so the current reconstruction defines a convex combination. 

## The Jensen majorant is separable

We get

$$
\sum_j \lambda_{i,j}u_{i,j}
= \sum_j U[i,j]x[j] = (Ux)[i].
$$

Therefore the Jensen bound is the majorant

$$
\xi(x,x^{(k)})
= \sum_{i,j}\frac{U[i,j]x^{(k)}[j]}{\hat y[i]}
f\left(y[i],\frac{x[j]}{x^{(k)}[j]}\hat y[i]\right).
$$

Each term depends on only one coefficient $x[j]$, so the minimization separates across $j$.

## From the majorant to MU

For every coefficient $x[j]$, set the derivative of the majorant to zero:

$$
0=\sum_i U[i,j]
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}
\left(y[i],\frac{x[j]}{x^{(k)}[j]}\hat y[i]\right).
$$

The two losses give two scalar equations:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

**Euclidean loss**

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=z-y
$$

$$
x^{(k+1)}
=x^{(k)}\ast\frac{U^Ty}{U^TUx^{(k)}}.
$$

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

**KL divergence**

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=1-\frac{y}{z}
$$

$$
x^{(k+1)}
=x^{(k)}\ast
\frac{U^T(y/(Ux^{(k)}))}{U^T1}.
$$

:::
::::

## MM guarantees descent

Because the surrogate is tight at the current iterate,

$$
 f(x^{(k+1)})
\leq \xi(x^{(k+1)},x^{(k)})
\leq \xi(x^{(k)},x^{(k)})
= f(x^{(k)}).
$$

MU decreases the objective, but descent alone does not guarantee a fast rate or a unique limit point.

## Positivity and zero-locking

If an entry becomes exactly zero, multiplication keeps it zero forever. This is **zero-locking**.

A common safeguard is to enforce $x\geq\epsilon$:

$$
 x^{(k+1)} \leftarrow
 \max\left(x^{(k)}\ast\frac{\nabla^- f}{\nabla^+ f},\epsilon\right).
$$

Strict positivity also avoids division by zero and helps with the KL curvature near zero.

## Why MU is natural for NNKL

For Poisson data,

$$
Y[i]\mid x \sim \mathcal{P}((Ux)[i]).
$$

The latent contribution of component $j$ to observation $i$ is proportional to

$$
\frac{U[i,j]x[j]}{(Ux)[i]}.
$$

The EM algorithm updates these latent responsibilities, then re-estimates $x$. The resulting update is exactly NNKL MU.

# Rank-one approximations

## Rank-one KL approximation

For nonnegative $Y$, consider

$$
\min_{w,h\geq 0} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Y,wh^T).
$$

The optimal scaling conditions imply

$$
 h^*[j]\sum_i w^*[i] = \sum_i Y[i,j],
$$

and

$$
 w^*[i]\sum_j h^*[j] = \sum_j Y[i,j].
$$

Thus the rank-one factors are proportional to the column and row marginals of $Y$.

## Rank-one Frobenius approximation

For nonnegative $Y$,

$$
\min_{w,h\geq 0}\|Y-wh^T\|_F^2
$$

is solved by the leading rank-one SVD approximation, made nonnegative by taking absolute values of the leading singular vectors.

The Perron-Frobenius theorem guarantees nonnegative leading singular vectors for positive matrices.

## What to remember

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

**NNLS**

- cone projection
- KKT support conditions
- Active-Set for sparse vectors
- HALS for matrix updates

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

**NNKL**

- Poisson likelihood
- difficult curvature near zero
- optimal scaling
- MU and EM

:::
::::

## The optimization core of nonnegative LRA

Lecture 1 gave the model:

$$
\min_{W,H\geq 0} \|Y-WH^T\|_F^2.
$$

Lecture 2 opened the inner loop:

$$
\min_{x\geq 0} f(y,Wx).
$$

The same regression problems reappear inside NMF, nonnegative CP, nonnegative Tucker, and many other structured models.
